title: What is good oracy?
author: Daisy Christodoulou et al.
summary: Daisy Christodoulou and Chris Wheadon ask how oracy, the capacity to use and understand speech, can be assessed well given its practical and philosophical challenges. They note that spoken performance is harder to capture than writing and that holistic assessment suffers from marker unreliability, vague criteria and stereotyping rubrics, which helped lead England's regulator to drop speaking and listening from GCSE English in 2013. Their move is to look at Norway, where oracy has been taught and assessed since 1883 without standards statements or external tests, because teachers hold it as an unspoken construct in their professional knowledge. Teacher definitions and a description of progression from talking about a teddy bear to analysing Knut Hamsun suggest progression comes from more complex ideas. The authors then propose to replicate their approach to writing: gather oracy samples, have teachers judge them using Comparative Judgement, and build a community view of what good oracy is. The piece is short and ends as a recruitment note for a research project, so it is more a research design than a settled argument.
points: Oracy assessment is hard because speech is harder to capture than writing, takes time to administer, and holistic judgement brings unreliable markers and vague criteria.
England removed speaking and listening from the GCSE English grade in 2013, which sparked renewed interest in more robust assessment.
Norway has taught and assessed oracy since 1883 without standards or external tests, relying on teachers' shared, unspoken understanding.
Norwegian teachers see progression as coming from engaging with more complex ideas, something generic statements of attainment can miss.
The authors plan to build a scale of oracy through Comparative Judgement of samples by teachers, as they did for writing.
quotes: If we want to assess oracy using authentic tasks that are assessed holistically, we face the typical problems of such assessments: marker unreliability, vague assessment criteria, and rubrics which stereotype responses. Some of these issues contributed to the 2013 decision by Ofqual, the exam regulator in England, to remove the speaking and listening element from the final English GCSE grade.

In England we like to define constructs and create external assessments from those constructs. However, that’s not the only possible approach. In Norway, schools have been teaching and assessing oracy since 1883 and this is achieved without either statements of standards or external assessments.

Rather, oracy is seen to exist as an unspoken construct in the teachers’ knowledge base. While there are some doubts as to the precise definition of oracy, teachers are able to offer working definitions of what they are teaching.

Regarding quality of progression, some teachers are clear that this can be assessed, and suggest that it can come from the discussion of more complex ideas. This is something that can often be missed when working with generic statements of attainment.

Comparative Judgement will allow us to start building a scale of oracy which we can then examine qualitatively in conjunction with the teachers, so we can develop a community view of what good oracy is.
We didn’t set out any guidelines for teachers on what good writing should look like; instead, we allowed the teachers to build the construct of good writing through their professional judgements.
